result.markdown: --- title: "Interpolation" subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl and Dierckx.jl" engine: julia --- Interpolation of a difficult function from uniformly spaced samples: the convolution kernels against the cubic B-spline of Interpolations.jl, the B-spline interpolants of BSplineKit.jl at cubic and high order, and the quintic FITPACK spline of Dierckx.jl. First the accuracy as the grid is refined, then the time to construct an interpolant and the time to evaluate it, in one and two dimensions, and finally the two together: the time each method needs to reach a given accuracy. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Packages and the methods"} using ConvolutionInterpolations import Interpolations # qualified: exports `interpolate`, as BSplineKit does import BSplineKit import Dierckx using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie # each method maps (x, y) on a uniform grid to a callable interpolant methods_1d = [ "Interpolations.jl cubic" => (x, y) -> Interpolations.scale( Interpolations.interpolate(y, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), x), "BSplineKit k=4" => (x, y) -> BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(4)), "BSplineKit k=8" => (x, y) -> BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(8)), "Dierckx k=5" => (x, y) -> Dierckx.Spline1D(collect(x), collect(y); k = 5), "ConvInterp :a4" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :a4), "ConvInterp :b5" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b5), "ConvInterp :b7" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7), ] runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2) # Runge's function xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001); # fine points for measuring the error ``` ::: ## Convergence The largest error against Runge's function on the fine points, as the number of samples doubles: ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The convergence study"} ns = [21, 41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281] hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1) errs = Dict(name => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods_1d) for n in ns x = range(-1, 1, length = n) y = runge.(x) for (name, m) in methods_1d itp = m(x, y) push!(errs[name], maximum(abs.(itp.(xr) .- runge.(xr)))) end end fig = Figure(size = (800, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true, xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error") for (name, _) in methods_1d scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errs[name], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name) end lines!(ax, hs, errs["ConvInterp :b7"][end] .* (hs ./ hs[end]) .^ 7; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "slope 7") Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | | observed order | error at the finest grid | |:--|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl cubic | 2.03 | 1.8e-08 | | BSplineKit k=4 | 4.07 | 2.3e-10 | | BSplineKit k=8 | 8.27 | 4.4e-16 | | Dierckx k=5 | 6.12 | 1.1e-14 | | ConvInterp :a4 | 4.10 | 2.3e-10 | | ConvInterp :b5 | 6.65 | 1.1e-14 | | ConvInterp :b7 | 7.12 | 2.6e-15 | The cubic methods — Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit at order 4, and `:a4` — converge at 4th order; Dierckx's quintic at 6th, as does `:b5`; BSplineKit at order 8 and `:b7` at 7th. The difference between the last two is not the order but what it costs, which the timings show. ## Setup and query Construction time for a grid of a thousand samples, and evaluation time per point at a million random points, each interpolant built once and evaluated in one broadcast: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The 1D timings"} rng = MersenneTwister(1) n1 = 1000 x1 = range(-1, 1, length = n1) y1 = runge.(x1) p1 = rand(rng, 1_000_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99 # a million random points inside the grid rows_1d = map(methods_1d) do (name, m) t_setup = (@b $m($x1, $y1)).time itp = m(x1, y1) t_query = (@b $itp.($p1)).time / length(p1) (name = name, t_setup = t_setup, t_query = t_query) end; ``` ::: | | setup, 1000 samples | query, per point | |:--|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl cubic | 36.1 μs | 8 ns | | BSplineKit k=4 | 53.9 μs | 47 ns | | BSplineKit k=8 | 94.5 μs | 55 ns | | Dierckx k=5 | 132.7 μs | 220 ns | | ConvInterp :a4 | 3.2 μs | 5 ns | | ConvInterp :b5 | 2.8 μs | 8 ns | | ConvInterp :b7 | 3.1 μs | 11 ns | In two dimensions, a 200 × 200 grid and two hundred thousand random points. Interpolations.jl and Dierckx have tensor-product interpolants; BSplineKit's are one-dimensional, so it is not in this table: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The 2D timings"} n2 = 200 x2 = range(-1, 1, length = n2) y2 = range(-1, 1, length = n2) z2 = [runge(xi) * runge(yi) for xi in x2, yi in y2] px = rand(rng, 200_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99 py = rand(rng, 200_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99 methods_2d = [ "Interpolations.jl cubic" => () -> Interpolations.scale( Interpolations.interpolate(z2, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), x2, y2), "Dierckx k=5" => () -> Dierckx.Spline2D(collect(x2), collect(y2), z2; kx = 5, ky = 5), "ConvInterp :a4" => () -> convolution_interpolation((x2, y2), z2; kernel = :a4), "ConvInterp :b5" => () -> convolution_interpolation((x2, y2), z2; kernel = :b5), "ConvInterp :b7" => () -> convolution_interpolation((x2, y2), z2; kernel = :b7), ] rows_2d = map(methods_2d) do (name, m) t_setup = (@b $m()).time itp = m() t_query = if itp isa Dierckx.Spline2D (@b Dierckx.evaluate($itp, $px, $py)).time / length(px) # Dierckx evaluates point lists through `evaluate` else (@b $itp.($px, $py)).time / length(px) end (name = name, t_setup = t_setup, t_query = t_query) end; ``` ::: | | setup, 200 × 200 samples | query, per point | |:--|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl cubic | 494.6 μs | 22 ns | | Dierckx k=5 | 1.54 ms | 199 ns | | ConvInterp :a4 | 68.1 μs | 20 ns | | ConvInterp :b5 | 84.8 μs | 31 ns | | ConvInterp :b7 | 103.3 μs | 40 ns | The convolution interpolants compute nothing at construction beyond the boundary values, and evaluate in a fixed number of operations per point — the stencil's — whatever the grid size, with the cell located by one division per axis. A B-spline interpolant solves a banded system at construction and searches for the cell at evaluation; a FITPACK spline does both in Fortran. The tables show where each trade lands. ## Time to accuracy When the samples are given, the convergence plot is the measure: the error at that grid is what you get. When the sampling is yours to choose — a table you generate, output you resample — the question becomes which method reaches a given accuracy in the least time, and a finer grid is allowed if it pays. The work–precision diagram puts the two together: for each method and each grid of the convergence study, the time to construct the interpolant and evaluate it at a hundred thousand points, against the error on that grid. A curve further left reaches the same accuracy in less time. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The work–precision study"} pw = rand(rng, 100_000) .* 1.98 .- 0.99 # the evaluation workload times = Dict(name => Float64[] for (name, _) in methods_1d) for n in ns x = range(-1, 1, length = n) y = runge.(x) for (name, m) in methods_1d push!(times[name], (@b begin itp = $m($x, $y); itp.($pw) end).time) end end fig = Figure(size = (800, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate at 10⁵ points [s]", ylabel = "largest error") for (name, _) in methods_1d scatterlines!(ax, times[name], max.(errs[name], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = name) end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Each curve descends as its grid refines, and the curves are nearly vertical: at a hundred thousand evaluations the time is the evaluation, for every method, and a finer grid costs almost nothing. A method's position left to right is therefore its cost per point, and the depth of its curve is how far its order takes it. The spline of order 8 needs fewer samples than `:b7` for a given error and reaches rounding later; the cubic B-spline and `:b5` cost the same per point, and `:b5` goes five decades deeper. The kernels are first to any accuracy down to rounding, which is the trade they were designed for. --- *Rendered with Julia 1.13.3 on a Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700KF machine (28 threads), with ConvolutionInterpolations.jl 1.0.2, Interpolations.jl 0.16.3, BSplineKit.jl 0.19.3, Dierckx.jl 0.5.4, FastChebInterp.jl 1.3.1, NumericalIntegration.jl 0.3.4, HCubature.jl 1.8.0, QuadGK.jl 2.11.3, ScatteredInterpolation.jl 0.3.6, NaturalNeighbours.jl 1.3.6, Chairmarks.jl 1.3.1.*
